title: X-Mode sold location data that could reveal visits to clinics and places of worship
hook: Apps you never thought about were reporting where you go.
collected: Precise location data from phones, gathered through X-Mode's software kit inside other companies' apps and from other suppliers.
howObtained: Apps that included X-Mode's SDK shared location with it; some users had allowed location for the app's own purpose.
inferred: Visits to medical and reproductive health clinics, places of worship and domestic-abuse shelters.
done: The FTC alleged X-Mode (later Outlogic) sold raw location data that could track people to such places, including to government contractors.
affected: People using apps carrying the SDK.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: First FTC order banning a data broker from selling sensitive location data; it also covers LGBTQ+ service locations and protest sites.

sources.title: FTC Order Prohibits Data Broker X-Mode Social and Outlogic from Selling Sensitive Location Data

limits: The order restricts future conduct; the full list of past buyers is not public.
whyItMatters: Allowing location for a weather or prayer app can mean your movements are sold onward.

title: InMarket built audiences like "wealthy and not healthy"
hook: Location data turned into nearly 2,000 shopping and life-stage lists.
collected: Precise location from InMarket's own apps and its SDK in other apps.
howObtained: Users granted location to apps, often for shopping rewards.
inferred: Segments such as "Christian church goers", "parents of preschoolers" and "wealthy and not healthy".
done: The FTC alleged InMarket used the data to place people in nearly 2,000 advertising audiences without properly telling them.
affected: Users of InMarket and partner apps.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: First FTC ban on a company selling or licensing precise location data.

sources.title: FTC Order Will Ban InMarket from Selling Precise Consumer Location Data

limits: The segment names come from the FTC complaint; how often each list was used is not public.
whyItMatters: These segment names are real. They show how a profile is built from where you go.

title: Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla: sensitive places and protest attendance
hook: Location from ad auctions was used to profile visitors to health clinics, churches and protests.
collected: Location data, including from real-time bidding (ad auctions) where apps broadcast data to many bidders.
howObtained: Mobilewalla collected data from ad auctions even when it did not win the bid, according to the FTC.
inferred: Visits to healthcare facilities and places of worship; for Mobilewalla, pregnancy-centre visitors and people who attended protests, profiled by city and race (per FTC complaint and secondary summaries).
done: The FTC alleged both companies sold or used these sensitive inferences.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC final orders (Gravy 5-0; Mobilewalla split vote). No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: Final orders banning the sale of sensitive location data; the first FTC claim that harvesting ad-auction data is itself unfair.

sources.title: FTC Finalizes Order Prohibiting Gravy Analytics, Venntel from Selling Sensitive Location Data
FTC Finalizes Orders Against Data Brokers Over Sensitive Location Data

limits: Some segment details for Mobilewalla come from secondary summaries of the complaint.
whyItMatters: Ad auctions broadcast your data to many companies at once, and not only the winner keeps it.

title: FTC v. Kochava ends with limits on sensitive location data
hook: A four-year fight over whether selling location data is itself harmful.
collected: Precise location linked to mobile advertising IDs from millions of devices.
howObtained: Bought from apps and other suppliers.
inferred: Visits to reproductive health clinics, places of worship, shelters and addiction-recovery centres, according to the FTC.
done: The FTC sued in 2022, alleging Kochava sold data that could identify people and track them to sensitive places.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC-approved stipulated order (2-0). We could not confirm the court had entered it as of November 2026.

outcome.text: Order requiring consent for sensitive location data, a sensitive-locations program, supplier checks and data deletion. No money.

sources.title: FTC v. Kochava, Inc. case page
FTC Remains on the Location Data Beat

limits: Ended in an injunction only, so a court never ruled on the core question.
whyItMatters: The company argued that selling data nobody had yet misused caused no harm. That question is still open.

title: "Twelve Million Phones, One Dataset, Zero Privacy"
hook: Journalists given a leaked location file could follow named officials home.
collected: More than 50 billion location pings from more than 12 million US phones in 2016-17.
howObtained: Leaked to The New York Times by sources at a location-data company.
inferred: Home and work addresses, routines, identities.
done: Reporters showed the 'anonymous' data could be used to identify and follow specific people, including officials.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative journalism with an explained method.

outcome.text: No direct enforcement; widely cited in later regulation debates.

sources.title: Twelve Million Phones, One Dataset, Zero Privacy

limits: Paywalled; we could not open the original. The source company was not named.
whyItMatters: "Anonymous" location data stops being anonymous once you can see where a phone sleeps at night.

title: Prayer app location data and the US military supply chain
hook: Reporting traced data from a Muslim prayer app through a broker toward military contractors.
collected: Location data from users of Muslim Pro, a prayer and Quran app.
howObtained: The app included X-Mode's software kit.
done: Motherboard (Vice) reported that X-Mode sold location data that reached US military contractors.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative journalism. The FTC's 2024 X-Mode order separately confirmed sales to government contractors in general, not this specific claim.

companyResponse.text: Muslim Pro called the report incorrect and untrue, denied selling data directly to the military, and stopped working with X-Mode.
companyResponse.source: Muslim Pro statement, via press coverage

outcome.text: Apple and Google banned the X-Mode SDK from their app stores in December 2020.

sources.title: How the U.S. Military Buys Location Data from Ordinary Apps
US military buys location data of Muslim apps

limits: The full data path was not independently confirmed, and the app disputes the report.
whyItMatters: Religious apps can reveal religion, even though you never typed it in anywhere.

title: A priest outed using commercially available app data
hook: A Catholic news outlet used bought app-signal data to link a named priest to Grindr use.
collected: App-signal and location data, said to be commercially available, from an unnamed vendor.
howObtained: Obtained by The Pillar; the exact source and method were never disclosed.
inferred: That a specific person used a gay dating app and where.
done: The Pillar published the findings, and the priest resigned.
affected: Monsignor Jeffrey Burrill, and anyone whose app data is sold.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: A news outlet's own report. Its method was not disclosed, and its ethics are widely CONTESTED.

companyResponse.text: Grindr called it an "unethical, homophobic witch hunt" and said it doubted the data came from Grindr.

outcome.text: No legal outcome; widely cited as the first public case of broker data used to out a named person.

sources.title: Priest outed via Grindr app highlights rampant data tracking

limits: The method was not disclosed, so it cannot be checked. Experts called the report vague.
whyItMatters: Shows how commercial data can harm one specific, real person.

title: Arizona v. Google: location tracked after users turned it off
hook: Turning off 'Location History' did not stop all location collection, the state alleged.
collected: Location data, including through settings other than 'Location History' (such as 'Web & App Activity').
done: Arizona's attorney general alleged Google misled users into thinking that switching off Location History stopped location tracking.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: State attorney-general settlement. Google did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: Google said the case concerned outdated product policies it had changed years earlier, and pointed to its controls and auto-delete options.

sources.title: Google to Pay $85 Million to Settle Arizona Geolocation Tracking Privacy Suit

limits: Settled; the allegations were not tested at trial.
whyItMatters: Privacy settings can mean less than their names suggest.

title: Texas v. Google: location, voiceprints and face data ($1.375 billion)
hook: Texas's largest privacy settlement with Google covered location, Incognito and biometrics.
collected: Location data, Incognito-mode browsing, and voiceprints and face geometry, according to the state.
done: Texas alleged Google collected and used this data without proper consent under state law.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: State attorney-general settlement. Google did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: Google said the settlement resolved old claims about policies it had already changed: "We are pleased to put them behind us, and we will continue to build robust privacy controls."

sources.title: Google to pay Texas $1.375 billion over privacy violations

limits: The settlement terms were not fully disclosed.
whyItMatters: State laws, not only federal ones, now drive big privacy outcomes in the US.
